title: Two variables at once
objectives: Plot one return series against another and read the relationship
Compare two prices on one rebased axis instead of two scales

screens.title: One dot per day
screens.prose: Each dot is one trading day. Across is the market's return that day; up is ACME's return. A chart of one variable against another is a **scatter plot**.
screens.question: Tap the day the **market** fell the most.

hints.text: The market's return is read across, along the x axis.
The market's worst day is the dot furthest left.
The dot at −2.1% across is the market's worst day.

feedback.correct: The market fell 2.1% that day, and ACME fell 2.4%.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the market along the horizontal axis.

byKey.p1: That is the lowest dot: ACME's worst day, −3.0%. The market only fell 1.2% then. The market is read across, not up.

explain.text: You read across for the market and found the dot furthest left. The lowest dot is a different day: ACME fell 3.0% while the market fell 1.2%, news of its own.

screens.title: A line through the cloud
screens.prose: The orange line through the origin predicts ACME's return as slope × the market's return. The coloured sticks are its misses, and the readout adds up their squares. Move the slope.
screens.question: Which slope makes the squared misses smallest?

widget.label: Slope
widget.accept: 1.3, or 1.2 to 1.4: the exact best slope through the origin is 1.33.

feedback.correct: Close to 1.3: ACME moves about 1.3 times as far as the market.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Slide until the total of squared misses stops falling.

byKey.one: A slope of 1 says ACME moves just like the market. The misses shrink further above 1.
byKey.start: That is where the slider started. Move it and watch the total.

explain.text: You found the slope where the squared misses bottom out, about 1.3. The best value, $\sum xy / \sum x^2 = 21.88 / 16.5 = 1.33$, sits between your slider steps.

screens.title: What the slope means
screens.prose: That slope is ACME's **beta** to the market: how far ACME tends to move for each 1% the market moves. Here beta is about 1.3.
screens.question: On a day the market falls 2%, what return does the line predict for ACME?

hints.text: The line says ACME = slope × market.
Here the market is −2% and the slope 1.3.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply the market's return by the slope.

byKey.sign: The market fell, so a positive slope predicts a fall for ACME too.
byKey.same: That assumes a slope of 1. ACME moves 1.3 times as far.
byKey.divide: You divided by the slope. The line multiplies the market's return by it.

explain.text: Reading the line at −2% across gives −2.6% up. A beta above 1 means the stock tends to amplify the market's moves, in both directions.

screens.title: Prices against prices

screens.question: The top plot shows a tight rising line. What does it tell you?

options.text: Little: both prices trended up, so any two rising prices line up
The two stocks move together month by month
options.why: You read the price plot as a link between the stocks. Their returns, in the bottom plot, show no pattern.

options.text: DELTA has a beta of about 0.3 to ACME
options.why: A slope fitted to price levels measures the two trends, not how the stocks react to each other.

hints.text: What do the two price series have in common?
Both rose over the year. Time is hiding inside both axes.
Plot returns to remove the trend: the bottom plot is a shapeless cloud.

feedback.correct: Shared trends make prices line up, whatever the link.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare the left plot with the returns on the right.

explain.text: Prices against prices mostly shows that both trended: their correlation is 0.95. Their monthly returns have a correlation of 0.05, close to none. Scatter returns against returns, never price against price.

import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")  # draw to files, not a window
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt


def returns_scatter(mkt, stock):
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5, 5))
    ax.scatter(mkt, stock)
    ax.set_xlabel("Market return")
    ax.set_ylabel("ACME return")
    return fig, ax

tests.call: [[round(float(v), 4) for v in p] for p in ax.collections[0].get_offsets()]

screens.title: Colours anyone can read
screens.prose: About one man in twelve has some colour blindness, most often between red and green. This chart uses the app's first three palette colours and names each line at its end.
screens.question: Select all that apply: which choices help a colour-blind reader tell the lines apart?

options.text: A name at the end of each line
Blue, orange and aqua from a palette checked for colour blindness
No more than three lines on one chart
Red for one stock and green for another
options.why: Red against green is the commonest confusion. Those two lines could look the same.

options.text: A legend box with six colour swatches
options.why: A legend makes the reader match colours back and forth, and six colours cannot all stay distinct.

hints.text: Which choices still work if two colours look alike?
A label needs no colour matching at all.
Direct labels, a checked palette and few lines all help; red against green and a six-swatch legend do not.

feedback.correct: Labels, a checked palette and few lines.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Imagine two of the colours looking the same, and ask what still works.

byKey.redgreen: Red against green is exactly the pair most colour-blind readers confuse.
byKey.legend: Six swatches in a box ask the reader to match colours, the hardest task for them.

explain.text: A label at each line's end works even when colours fail, so it beats a legend. A checked palette keeps neighbouring colours apart, and three lines keep the chart readable.

screens.title: Two axes, one crossing
screens.prose: A popular way to show two prices at once: ACME on the left axis, BETA on a second axis on the right (`ax.twinx()`). Both charts plot the same monthly closes. Only BETA's right-hand axis range differs.
screens.question: In which month did BETA overtake ACME?

options.text: Neither chart can say: each crossing comes from the axis range someone chose
Month 2, as the top chart shows
options.why: You read the crossing as an event. Change BETA's axis range and the crossing moves, as the bottom chart shows.

options.text: Month 8, as the bottom chart shows
options.why: That crossing is real only for that axis range. The top chart puts it in month 2 with the same data.

hints.text: The data are the same in both charts. What differs?
Only BETA's axis range changed, and the crossing moved.
ACME trades near £125 and BETA near £50. One cannot overtake the other in price.

feedback.correct: The crossing is an artefact of the second axis.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask why the two charts disagree.

byKey.m2: You read the crossing as a moment BETA got ahead. Change BETA's axis range and the crossing jumps to month 8. With two axes, crossings mean nothing.
byKey.m8: You trusted the second chart's crossing. The first chart, same data, puts it in month 2. With two axes, crossings mean nothing.

explain.text: A second axis lets the chart maker slide and stretch one line at will, so crossings and gaps are set by choice. To compare two prices, rebase both to 100 on one axis instead.

screens.title: One axis for two prices
screens.prose:
Rebasing divides each price by its first value and multiplies by 100, so both lines start at 100 on one axis. Every point then reads as growth of £100.

$$R_t = 100 \times \frac{p_t}{p_0}$$

```python
rebased = [100 * p / prices[0] for p in prices]
```
screens.question: BETA went from £48.00 to £52.80. Where does its rebased line end?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide the last price by the first, then multiply by 100.

byKey.diff: You added the £4.80 rise to 100. Rebasing scales by the ratio: 52.80 / 48.00 = 1.1.
byKey.ratio: That is the ratio. Multiply by 100 to put it on the rebased scale.

explain.text: BETA ends at 110 and ACME at $100 \times 128.50 / 120.00 = 107.08$. On one shared axis, BETA's lead is real: 10% against 7.1%. No axis was chosen to make it so.

widget.solution:
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")  # draw to files, not a window
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt


def rebased_chart(a, b, names):
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4.5))
    for prices, name, colour in zip([a, b], names, ["#2A78D6", "#EB6834"]):
        r = [100 * p / prices[0] for p in prices]
        ax.plot(r, color=colour)
        ax.text(len(r) - 1, r[-1], " " + name, color=colour, va="center")
    ax.set_ylabel("Rebased to 100")
    return fig, ax

feedback.correct: One axis, two named lines, colours a colour-blind reader can separate.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the failing test: it names what it checked.

explain.text: Both lines start at 100, so their gap is a real difference in growth: BETA +10%, ACME +2.5%. The names sit where the eye already is, at the line ends.

ideas: A scatter of returns, market across and stock up, shows how a stock reacts; the slope of the best line is its beta.
Prices against prices line up whenever both trend. Scatter returns, not levels.
Two y axes let any crossing be set by choice. Rebase both prices to 100 on one axis, name each line at its end, and keep to three palette colours.

formula.name: Rebased to 100
formula.note: Every line starts at 100, so gaps between lines are differences in growth.

summary.trap: Where two lines cross on a dual-axis chart depends on the axis ranges, not the data.

quiz.question: What does it print?

options.why: `twinx` adds a second Axes that shares the x axis. The figure now holds two.
Each `plot` call adds a line, not an Axes. Only `twinx` added one.

feedback.correct: The twin is a second Axes on top of the first.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the Axes, not the lines.

explain.text: `ax.twinx()` makes a new Axes with its own y axis over the same x axis. That second, free y axis is what lets a chart maker move one line at will.

quiz.prose: A stock goes from £250.00 to £230.00 over a quarter.
quiz.question: Where does its line end when rebased to 100?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Scale by the ratio of last to first.

byKey.diff: You took the £20 fall away from 100. Rebasing uses the ratio, a fall of 8%.
byKey.ratio: That is the ratio. Multiply by 100.

explain.text: £230 is 92% of £250, so the rebased line ends at 92: an 8% fall.

quiz.prose: A scatter of daily returns, the market across and a utility stock up, has a best-fit slope of 0.5.
quiz.question: What does that tell you?

options.text: The stock tends to move about half as far as the market
The stock rises on half of the days
options.why: The slope is about the size of moves, not how often the stock rises.
Slope and correlation are different numbers. A tight cloud can have any slope.

options.text: The stock moves twice as far as the market
options.why: You divided the wrong way. A slope of 0.5 is half the market's move.

feedback.correct: A beta of 0.5: half the market's moves.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the slope as up-per-across.

explain.text: The slope says each 1% across comes with about 0.5% up. That is a beta of 0.5: a defensive stock that dampens the market's moves.

quiz.prose: An analyst scatters gold's price against a tech stock's price over ten years. The dots lie close to a line.
quiz.question: What should they plot instead to judge whether the two move together?

options.text: Gold's daily returns against the stock's daily returns
Both prices over time on two y axes
options.why: Two axes let the lines be placed anywhere. Any apparent link would be the analyst's choice.

options.text: The same scatter with log axes
options.why: Logs keep both trends, so the dots still line up.

options.text: The same scatter over twenty years
options.why: A longer history has longer trends. The dots line up even more.

feedback.correct: Returns remove the trends that make prices line up.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Remove the trend before comparing.

explain.text: Two assets that both rose over ten years line up as prices whatever their link. Daily returns strip out the trend, and their scatter shows whether the moves agree.
